figures.caption: Fig. 1. Comparison between existing method and ours. In the training phase, unlike existing supervised methods that rely on large-scale collections of forged faces, our FADNet requires only real face images for training. In the detection phase, Deepfake Detector exhibits strong performance primarily on Deepfakes but generalizes poorly to synthetic faces. Synthetic Detector performs well on synthetic faces but is less effective in detecting Deepfakes. Our method effectively identifies both Deepfakes and synthetic faces within a unified detection framework.

Fig. 4. Accuracy comparison between our FADNet and SOTA baselines on (a) DF40. and (b) ASFD. It is evident that FADNet occupies the most extensive region within the radar plot, demonstrating its superior overall performance profile across all evaluated metrics relative to the baselines.

Fig. 5. Comparative Grad-CAM visualizations of real versus forged faces. U represents uncertainty value. The top row displays the heatmaps of authentic faces, while the bottom row illustrates those of forged samples. It is evident that for real faces, the heatmaps are concentrated on core facial regions with a localized focus. In contrast, forged faces exhibit a more dispersed and irregular distribution. Furthermore, authentic faces yield lower uncertainty values.

Fig. 2. The overall architecture of FADNet. During the training phase, a PFIG is utilized to create pseudo-forgery samples, which are used in conjunction with real images to train FADNet. Once the training is complete, the model parameters are frozen. In the inference stage, authentic images yield low uncertainty values, whereas all other inputs generate high uncertainty values, thereby facilitating effective differentiation.

Fig. 6. Comparative t-SNE analysis of feature distributions between FADNet and SOTA approaches. The blue clusters represent real samples, while other colors denote various forgery types. In contrast to baseline models that rely on specific generator patterns, FADNet captures the intrinsic distribution of real faces. The absence of isolated clusters for different forgery types suggests that our model learns source-invariant features, which is key to its better detection performance.
Fig. 7. Ablation study of the decision threshold. The model achieves optimal accuracy and F1-score at a threshold of 0.691.

Fig. 3. Comparison between pristine images and their pseudo-forgery counterparts. These pseudo-forgery samples are derived from authentic images through various transformations, exhibiting diverse visual discrepancies.
